content: In a hinge joint, also known as a ginglymus, the articulating surfaces of the bones are shaped in such a way that they allow movement predominantly in a single plane. This movement is typically forward and backward, and the range of motion in this plane is often substantial. However, the motion of the distal bone during flexion rarely occurs in the exact same plane as the axis of the proximal bone. Instead, there is usually a slight deviation from a straight line during the process of flexion. The articulating surfaces of the bones in a hinge joint are connected by relatively weak collateral ligaments. These ligaments serve as the primary structures that maintain the union between the bones. The most representative examples of hinge joints include the interphalangeal joints (found in the fingers and toes) and the joint between the humerus and ulna at the elbow. The knee and ankle joints, while also classified as hinge joints, are less typical examples because they permit a small degree of rotational or side-to-side movement when the limb is in certain positions.
